desc:
A binary tree can be stored in an array the way a binary heap is: the root sits at index 0, and the node at index i keeps its left child at index 2i + 1 and its right child at index 2i + 2. Slots that belong to no node contain -1, and the array ends at the last real node (so its last entry is never -1).

Given a tree in the usual level-order encoding, return its heap-indexed array. The empty tree gives [].

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed (or returned) as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree below: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [1, -1, 2, -1, 3] (a chain that always goes right) the root is at index 0, node 2 at index 2 and node 3 at index 6, so the answer is [1, -1, 2, -1, -1, -1, 3]. For a perfect tree such as [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] the answer is the same array.
constraints: Every tree array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
The tree has at most 12 levels (so the answer has at most 4,095 entries)
hints: Every node has a fixed position in the heap layout that depends only on the path from the root to it.
If a node is at index i, its children are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2. So you only need to know the index of each node's parent.

Walk through the nodes in level order. Parents always come before their children, so you can compute each child's index when you process the parent, then allocate an array of size (largest index + 1) filled with -1.
editorial: Both encodings list the real nodes in level order, so converting between them is a bookkeeping exercise: find the parent of each node, apply 2i + 1 or 2i + 2, and drop the value into an array that was pre-filled with -1.

The children of the k-th real node occupy the slots 2k + 1 and 2k + 2 of the compact array, which tells us who the parent of every node is. The largest heap index belongs to a real node, so the array length is exactly that index plus one. The depth limit keeps the output small: a long right chain would otherwise need an exponentially large array, which is the reason heap layouts are only used for balanced-ish trees.
